det_01.label: The Appeal's first national commissary database
det_01.content: This dataset is 'Locked In, Priced Out,' the first national database of U.S. prison commissary prices, built by the nonprofit news outlet The Appeal and published April 17, 2024. Over a roughly nine-month investigation, reporters Ethan Corey and Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg filed public-records requests to all 50 state departments of corrections; 46 states provided usable commissary lists. The team standardized prices for 24 food, hygiene, and religious products across those states. A commissary is the prison store where incarcerated people buy goods beyond what the institution issues. Because people in prison cannot shop anywhere else, the commissary is a captive market with no competition.

det_02.label: Prison wages: pennies per hour
det_02.content: The buying power behind these prices is almost nothing. Wages for incarcerated workers nationally run roughly $0.14 to $0.63 per hour for most institutional jobs, and several states pay far less or nothing at all: Louisiana averages about $0.06 per hour, federal prison jobs pay about $0.12, and Texas pays its prison workers nothing. The Vera Institute documents wages as low as $0.06 to $0.24 per hour, with people working 6 to 8 hours a day, five days a week, yet earning only about $6 every two weeks. In Tennessee, wages of $0.17 to $0.50 per hour have not changed in over 30 years even as commissary prices track inflation. This is the benchmark that makes every commissary price in the dataset meaningful: a price of $1 is not $1 to someone earning six cents an hour.

det_03.label: Markups up to 600% over outside prices
det_03.content: The Appeal found commissary prices up to five times higher than community prices, with markups reaching 600%. State-specific markups documented include Arkansas marking up all items 40-50%, Missouri inflating ramen by more than 65%, and Georgia marking up peanut butter over 70%. California's markups previously ranged 63-200% before a cap of 35% was imposed through 2028; Michigan cut its food markup to 14% after eliminating hygiene markups. Ramen that costs about 30-35 cents at a retail store like Target sells for $0.24 to $1.06 in prison commissaries. A bar of soap can cost up to $2.80 in prison, roughly 23 hours of work at the lowest wage.

det_04.label: Vendors and kickback contracts
det_04.content: Prison commissaries are often run by private vendors who pay the state a commission on every sale, an incentive structure that pushes prices up rather than down. Keefe Group (controlled by private-equity firm HIG Capital) and Union Supply Group are the dominant national vendors; the dataset records vendors including 'Keefe Commissary' (16 states), 'State-run' (17 states), and 'Union Supply Group' (6 states). Florida's DOC receives a 35.6% commission from Keefe under a five-year, $175 million contract. Kentucky receives a 16% kickback from Union Supply Group. These commissions mean the state profits more when incarcerated people pay more, aligning the interests of the prison and the vendor against the buyer.

det_05.label: Religious items cost far more than secular equivalents
det_05.content: The investigation surfaced a striking pattern in religious goods: items central to minority faiths are often priced well above Christian equivalents or secular near-equivalents. In Connecticut, a Bible sold for $4.55 while the Noble Quran cost $25.99. In Virginia, a Christmas card cost $0.80 while a Ramadan card cost $2.33. In Tennessee, a designated prayer rug cost $17.95 while an ordinary floor rug cost under $6.00. Because religious practice is a protected right, these disparities raise questions about equal access to faith for incarcerated people of non-Christian religions.

det_06.label: Headline product examples from the investigation
det_06.content: The Appeal foregrounded a handful of products that dramatize the problem. A pair of reading glasses cost more than $15 in Vermont prisons, about five times the Walgreens price. An 8-inch plastic fan cost nearly $40 at Delaware's Sussex Correctional Institution, $29.95 in Mississippi, and around $33 in Indiana, a major expense in facilities that are often dangerously hot and lack air conditioning. These items are not luxuries: reading glasses, hygiene products, and fans are basic health needs that the institution does not provide for free, forcing reliance on the commissary.

det_07.label: Caveats: what the data can and cannot show
det_07.content: Two cautions for the analyst. First, the database reflects lists from a single point in time (effective dates cluster around 2023-2024) and 46 of 50 states; four states (including Alabama) provided no usable list, so absence of a state is missing data, not a zero price. Second, the 'cheapest_price' and 'common_option' fields in the summary table were selected by The Appeal's editors to enable apples-to-apples comparison across states, so a state's listed cheapest ramen is the cheapest comparable product they could identify, not necessarily the only one sold. Prices are stored as strings with a leading dollar sign and must be cleaned before numeric analysis. Cross-state spread is the most defensible headline finding because it compares the same product type across states using the same selection method.
